I'm Madelyn, a planning student asking how places can work for the people who live in them.

I'm a graduate student in Community and Regional Planning at UT Austin with a GIS background, and my research focuses on housing and community in Flint. I pair spatial analysis with time spent on the ground.

See my projects Say hello

Why housing

During my internship at SIPI, I shadowed community leaders in Flint neighborhoods where fires, crime, and other problems that follow vacant properties are part of everyday life. "Blight" is the word people there use. It's a heavy word, but it points to something real.

I also came away understanding how fragile housing is for low-income families, and how little protection and few resources exist to keep it stable, especially in Flint.

That's what I'm bringing into the Master of Science in Community and Regional Planning (MSCRP) program at UT Austin.

How can we do better research on these communities, and make sure meaningful impact reaches the groups most affected?

Projects

Mapping community assets and service gaps in Flint

SIPI Inc., Flint, Michigan. GIS Intern, June to August 2025.

I led SIPI's Community Asset Mapping Initiative, designing and building an interactive map of Flint's community assets. It brings together local data on food access, mental health resources, and grassroots organizations. It's now used across SIPI's network of community partners to identify service gaps and inform collaborative investments, and it supports local nonprofits and small businesses.

The map didn't rely on data alone. I shadowed leaders in government, nonprofit, and community organizations to understand Flint's socioeconomic landscape, then combined what I learned with the spatial data to inform equitable resource allocation and strategic planning.

Tools. Esri products, QGIS, qgis2web, qualitative research

Keeping park data current in the field

City of Garland Parks and Recreation, Garland, Texas. GIS Intern, August 2025 to January 2026.

I collected and updated park data in the field using Trimble GPS equipment and Esri FieldMaps, then maintained the spatial data in the citywide database. At the new Bob Day Tennis Complex, I helped build the whole site in the city's geodatabase from scratch after construction finished, locating everything from sprinkler heads to utility boxes in the field.

I also used Esri products to create and update layouts for park projects. One example is the Duck Creek Greenbelt park sign, which brings park rules, emergency contacts, a trail map, an amenities legend, and links to city resources together for five connected parks.

Tools. Trimble, FieldMaps, Esri products

Finding the “Social Anchor”: site selection in downtown Flint

GIS course project, GISC 4385, UT Dallas, May 2026.

For a hypothetical hospitality entrepreneur, I used network analysis to find where a new bar could reach students from the University of Michigan-Flint, Kettering University, and Mott Community College on foot. I built 5, 10, and 15-minute walking service areas, then layered on Gen Z population estimates, a drinking population prominence index, and the locations of 76 existing bars.

The analysis pointed to the blocks between UM-Flint and the MSU Extension as the strongest site. They sit inside the 5-minute walking zone, are zoned Downtown Core, and fall in the highest prominence zone. I also compared two alternatives, wrote about the limits of the data, and reflected on the responsibility that comes with recommending where investment should go in a city that is still recovering.

Tools. ArcGIS Pro, network analysis, Esri Enrichment, Business Analyst

McCabe and Ellen (2016), on how historic district designation changes New York City neighborhoods.

Mixed-income housing

Chaskin and Joseph (2013), on how residents experience mixed-income developments in Chicago.

Vacant property in Flint

Dewar (2015), on what happens to tax-foreclosed property in Detroit and Flint after different types of sales.

Housing revitalization in Flint In progress

Developing toward a thesis proposal in my research design class, UT Austin.

I'm exploring how Flint can revitalize its housing while preserving historic character and keeping neighborhoods open to all residents. My focus areas are historic preservation, mixed-income housing, and blighted and vacant properties.

In my research design class, I'm building this idea toward a thesis proposal. I compared three studies that each take on one piece of the puzzle, and the lesson I took from them is that a design is only as strong as its fit to the question. A quantitative panel is best at isolating a relationship, interviews explain how a policy is experienced, and field-based case studies show what actually happens on the ground.

I travel to Flint often, so in-person field research is something I'm open to alongside spatial analysis.

Questions that challenge my work

  • How can we make sure everybody has access?
  • How can we reach the people with the least access?
  • How can we measure access?
  • What does preservation look like to different groups of people?
  • What are the modern struggles of housing?
  • What has stayed the same in housing struggles throughout history?

Internships

City of Garland Parks and Recreation

GIS Intern, Design and Development

August 2025 to January 2026

I worked on a GIS team of two, alongside my supervisor, managing the spatial data and mapping systems behind more than 2,800 acres of parkland, the trail network, and facilities like aquatic and recreation centers.

What I worked on

  • Designed the Duck Creek Greenbelt park sign and map, digitizing in ArcGIS Pro, pulling from city databases, and finishing the layout in Adobe Illustrator so visitors could navigate the trails and new amenities accurately.
  • Built a StoryMap of the city's 2026 Capital Improvement Projects, so the department could show where construction and renovations were happening and how they were progressing.
  • Built the new Bob Day Tennis Complex in the city's geodatabase from scratch once construction finished, using Trimble GPS equipment and FieldMaps to locate every feature in the field, from sprinkler heads to utility boxes. I also kept the citywide park database up to date.
  • Worked daily in ArcGIS Pro and ArcGIS StoryMaps while learning the city's data standards and management protocols.

Beyond my desk

I met with the City of Plano's parks department to compare how each city tracks its assets with OpenGov, attended an OpenGov event in Grapevine, and shadowed GIS staff in other departments, where I learned how central GIS supports 911 dispatch and emergency services. I also sat in on a GIS technician interview and helped interview a candidate for the streets department.

What I took away

I came in thinking of GIS as a technical task. I left understanding that spatial data doesn't exist in a vacuum. It only works when it's backed by clear communication and partnership across departments. Seeing how mapping shapes the design of public spaces is what pushed me toward graduate study in planning.

View the 2026 Capital Improvement Projects StoryMap, created with help from my mentor, Evelyn Esparza.

SIPI Inc.

GIS Intern, Flint, Michigan

June to August 2025

In Flint, I built a map of the city's community assets and paired it with research on the ground, so the results reflected how Flint actually works and not only what the data showed.

What I worked on

  • Led SIPI's Community Asset Mapping Initiative, designing and developing an interactive GIS map that brings together local data on food access, mental health resources, and grassroots organizations. It's now used across SIPI's network of community partners to identify service gaps and inform collaborative investments.
  • Conducted qualitative research on Flint's socioeconomic landscape by shadowing leaders from government, nonprofit, and community organizations.
  • Combined the spatial data with those on-the-ground insights to inform equitable resource allocation and strategic planning.

Why it mattered to me

My goal was to use GIS to highlight parts of Flint that might be overlooked, and to help organizations serve people more effectively through visual tools. Coming back to the city where I was born, after more than a decade in Dallas, gave me a fresh perspective on it.

About me

Flint, Michigan is my hometown, and I still go back often. It's the place my research keeps returning to.

At UT Dallas I studied geospatial information sciences with a minor in political science. My internships have paired spatial data with time on the ground: shadowing community leaders in Flint, and collecting park data across Garland. Now I'm at UT Austin studying community and regional planning, with a focus on sustainable urban development.

Outside of school, I'm getting to know Austin's thrift and vintage scene, which I've been exploring since I moved here in May. I also take long walks around Lady Bird Lake, and I share my home with two cats, Bailey and Louise.

My family lives in Michigan. They moved back after living in Texas since 2013, which leaves me as the only Texan in the family.
